newsitem.title: USA: Perot fails to inspire, running out of time.
newsitem.headline: Perot fails to inspire, running out of time.

text.p: His quirky, straight-talking style was a breath of fresh air in 1992 but Ross Perot's second presidential bid now appears dead in the water, shot down by doubts over his temperament and programmes.

With just one week left before the election, polls show Perot stuck firmly in single digits and many former supporters say the Texas billionaire's appeal, so strong four years ago when he won 19 percent of the popular vote, has worn thin.
In a series of interviews in Perot's home state of Texas, many voters said they thought the short-tempered businessman lacks the skills of compromise and consensus-building needed to run the country.

"The trouble with Perot isn't what he says. I think most people agree when he says no one in Washington is trying to fix the real problems. It's just him. I just think he'd be a terrible president," said Jacqueline Stewart, 34, a saleswoman from Dallas, where Perot has his business and political base.

Stewart said she and her husband both voted for Perot in 1992 but now believe he is doing more harm than good to the cause of third party politics. "We do need someone, or a new party, to shake things up but Perot gives independents a bad name. He wants things done his way, and only his way, and it can't work like that."
Others, less charitably, noted Perot's penchant for elaborate conspiracy theories and said they doubted whether he had the mental capacity for the presidency.

Officials at Perot's Reform Party say his campaign was unfairly crippled by his exclusion from the presidential debates but insist he will pick up most undecided voters and make a last-minute surge between now and Nov. 5.

Public interest in the Perot campaign is by all measures much lower than it was in 1992. Less than 5 percent of the 1 million people who signed petitions to get the Reform Party on the ballot across the country bothered to take part in voting for its presidential nominee and viewers for Perot's trademark half-hour "infomercials" are down sharply from four years ago.
Political analysts say voters are not as angry at the two major parties as they were in 1992 and Perot was hurt by picking little-known economist Pat Choate as his running mate.

Al Harris, a Dallas mechanic who still has a "Run Ross Run" sticker from the 1992 campaign on the back of his battered blue pickup truck, said Perot does not have the air of a winner this time around.

"You get the impression he's just going through the motions. He spends all the time complaining, there's nothing there to vote for," Harris said, adding that he would reluctantly cast his ballot for Republican Bob Dole next week.

An ugly battle with former Colorado Gov. Richard Lamm for the Reform Party's nomination got Perot's campaign off to a poor start in August and critics charge that, while he attacks the two main parties for failing to tackle the budget deficit and thorny issues like Social Security reform, Perot has not come up with many concrete policy proposals.

"He has done a great job of admiring the problems but nothing to offer solutions," John Pitney, a political science professor at Claremont McKenna College near Los Angeles, said. "He has gone from being a temporary phenomena to a permanent joke."
But the support of the hard core of anti-government independents who have stayed with Perot grows more intense the more he appears certain to come in a distant third.

"Mr. Perot is our only hope," Stewart Swacker, an elderly retired Navy captain, said outside the Reform Party's state offices in Dallas, where he and his wife dropped by to offer their support to campaign workers.
"There will be either a bloody revolution or a peaceful revolution in this country, and Mr. Perot is the peaceful revolutionary who will turn things around," he said.
